extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and practitioners of dramatic theory and poets/playwrights seeking guidance on composing tragedy
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing Aristotelian-style tragedy: how to choose characters, structure plot, and shape pity, fear, and katharsis so the drama attains unity, moral weight, and aesthetic purification of emotion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Katharsis (emotional purgation/purification)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy effects a katharsis — an expulsion or purification of the painful and disquieting elements in pity and fear, transforming the admixture of pain in real life into a refined, pleasurable satisfaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret katharsis as both relief (discharge) and clarification/purification: art expels the selfish, morbid elements of pity and fear so that the spectator attains a 'noble emotional satisfaction.' This is an aesthetic end, not a direct moral reform, though indirect moral influence may follow. See also musical katharsis analogy (Plutarch).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pity and fear must be combined
rubrics_metrics.description: The full tragic effect requires the union of pity and fear; Aristotle's requirement is pity and fear together rather than either alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While some tragedies may predominantly evoke one emotion, an inferior tragedy may excite only one. Balance the two so pity tempers fear (preventing narrow selfish terror) and fear tempers pity (preventing sentimentalism).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of pity
rubrics_metrics.description: Pity is 'a sort of pain at an evident evil of a destructive or painful kind in the case of somebody who does not deserve it,' involving a tacit reference to oneself (we might expect it to happen to us).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish Aristotelian pity (self-regarding sympathy for an undeserving sufferer or one suffering beyond his deserts) from pure altruistic compassion; use characters whose misfortunes can provoke this reflexive pity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of fear (tragic fear)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fear is 'a species of pain or disturbance arising from an impression of impending evil which is destructive or painful in its nature,' typically near and concerning ourselves; in tragedy, fear is modified — a reflex of pity and becomes an impersonal awe about human destiny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In dramatic presentation, fear is often not direct personal dread but an imaginative shudder elicited by identification with the hero and by seeing human fate; craft scenes so fear is felt as a general moral inevitableness rather than paralysing personal terror.

rubrics_metrics.name: Similarity/identification with the hero
rubrics_metrics.description: The tragic sufferer must be 'a man like ourselves' (similar in moral character) so the spectator can identify and make the hero's misfortunes their own; this likeness is crucial to evoke pity and fear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create a hero with enough shared human qualities for audience identification, enabling sympathetic thrill and the 'lifting out of himself' effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hero's moral character: neither flawless nor villainous
rubrics_metrics.description: The hero should not be perfectly virtuous nor consummate villainy; he is elevated in dignity yet possesses frailties and imperfections — a 'rich and full humanity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid a purely virtuous or purely monstrous protagonist; give the hero qualities that other men possess but blended more potently, so the fall is intelligible and the audience sympathises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social status/distance of hero
rubrics_metrics.description: The hero is raised above the audience in external dignity or station (a prince or famous man who falls from greatness), providing contrast and an ideal distance for universalisation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose protagonists with social prominence so the action transcends private life and attains public or universal significance; this helps remove petty self-interests and aids katharsis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universalizability / significance of subject matter
rubrics_metrics.description: The subject must admit of universalisation: dramatic action should be significant and extensible so that it reveals higher laws of human destiny rather than remaining a private, particular case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer actions whose consequences attach to larger issues (state, society, humanity). Avoid subjects confined to private, bourgeois existence that resist being generalised and thus hinder tragic fear and solemnity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of Action (organic unity)
rubrics_metrics.description: The first requirement is unity of action: a single, complete action (a whole with beginning, middle, end) whose parts are arranged in fixed order and structurally related so none can be removed or transposed without harm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design the plot as an inward organic whole: incidents must be causally/probably connected and contribute to a single major action rather than being episodic or biographical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate magnitude / suitable length
rubrics_metrics.description: The whole must have a certain magnitude sufficient for the natural development of the story — neither infinitely large nor infinitesimally small — so the mind's eye or memory can grasp it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the play long enough to evolve freely and fully to decisive change, but not so vast as to become a series of detached scenes (avoid epic scale like the Trojan war for tragedy). Use human memory and audience capacity as practical limits rather than arbitrary act counts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unity-of-hero fallacy / avoid biographical sweep
rubrics_metrics.description: Unity of plot is not unity of the hero's life; many incidents in one man's life do not make a single dramatic action and a biographical/historical sweep can replace dramatic interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not attempt to compress a whole life or numerous disparate actions into one tragedy; instead select the single action that provides organic unity and dramatic intelligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causal necessity and probability of events
rubrics_metrics.description: Successive incidents must be connected by an inward, causal bond — the law of necessary and probable sequence — so that decisive change of fortune arises from the plot itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure that major reversals and outcomes are the inevitable (or at least probable) consequences of preceding events; avoid arbitrary or unmotivated turns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition (anagnorisis) and reversal (peripeteia) as integrated devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Plots may employ recognition and reversal to intensify emotions, but these surprises must be woven into the plot and discovered as inevitable consequences of earlier events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use recognition and reversal to heighten tragic effect, but make them logically entailed by the plot so they feel both surprising and necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of deus ex machina and accident
rubrics_metrics.description: The unravelling or dénouement must arise out of the plot itself, not by recourse to deus ex machina or mere accident.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not resolve the action through external contrivance or late-stage inventions; endings must follow from the established causal chain (cf. Lessing's critique of weak fifth acts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exhibit suffering in comprehensive aspects
rubrics_metrics.description: Suffering should be exhibited in one of its comprehensive aspects so that deeds and fortunes attach themselves to larger issues and the spectator is lifted above the special case to universal law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray events and characters so their consequences are not merely personal but reflect broader human conditions; this supports the transformation of emotions into universalised, purified feelings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotions must be divested of selfish/material elements
rubrics_metrics.description: For emotions to be allayed and transformed into pleasurable calm, they must lose purely selfish and material elements and become part of a new, more universal order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft representation that removes egoistic taints from pity and fear (through distance, elevation of subject, and universal resonance) so the spectator's tumult resolves into refined pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of motives: caution with love as tragic motive
rubrics_metrics.description: Love, especially when exclusive and self-absorbed, resists kathartic treatment and is rarely a tragic motive unless embedded in broader social or public consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If using love as central motive, ensure it intersects with larger social obligations or public stakes (e.g., Romeo and Juliet's feud) so the action attains the necessary universality and consequence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic presentation modifies emotions (artificial conditions matter)
rubrics_metrics.description: The conditions of dramatic representation modify pity and fear: pity retains its object but fear is altered by imaginative transfer — becoming reflective, impersonal awe and a sense of moral inevitableness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploit the difference between real-life emotions and their dramatic refracted forms: stagecraft and imaginative distance convert personal dread into contemplative awe that contributes to katharsis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain close alliance between pity and fear (identification over time-distinction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pity and fear become closely interwoven in tragedy; their alliance depends more on close identification with the hero (shared humanity) than on temporal distinctions between impending vs. actual suffering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop identification and moral likeness between audience and hero so that pity and fear blend; do not rely solely on time-based distinctions to differentiate the emotions.
